                                                 Sand Exclusion
                                              Omar Y. Mohamed,




Abstract - A major issue for the deepwater high - rate gas completions in the Simian/Sienna
field off the coast of Egypt was the placement of an effective sand control completion in the
presence of highly reactive shalesshale’s.  Analysis showed the most productive completion
method to be an open- hole completion. , hHowever, this method presented a challenge as the
shale encountered during the  drilling phase was very reactive and could destabilize during
completion equipment placement or during pumpi ng operations such as gravel packing. One
of the most concerning obstacles ofA major concern regarding open- hole gravel packing is
exposed reactive shalesshale’s that can destabilize.  If the shale section of the well bore
swells or flakes off,  they the particles can prevent running of the gravel pack assembly to
bottom, plug screens and/or collapse into the wellbore to prevent complete gravel placement.
Isolating the shale section behind casing will solv e the problem. hH,owever this process most
often means having to reduce the screen size, to be used which may impede production. This
paper will discuss Athe completion design solution for this project, which using used two
newly developed technologies and other carefully selected proven techniques was applied to
minimize the risks of shale instability. A new design of an alternatea multi- path screen
system was chosen because of its ease of assemb ly, ability to transport   gravel pack slurry
past annular blockages such as collapsed shales, and its minimization of slurry exit velocity
from the alternate path tubes while packing.  Another new technology that was selected for
application was the use of a non-ionic visco-elastic surfactant (VES) fluid to transport the
gravel pack sand down hole.  This fluid was chosen for its shale stability properties, excellent
sand suspension properties and the high return permeability characteristics of the fluid.   The
paper will discuss the enabling technologies and discuss how their Aapplication of these
technologies and observing other best practices risks associated with gravel packing in an
open hole in the presence of reactive shales was mitigated risk and contributed to a successful
completion in a challenging deepwater environment.

Swelling Packer Technology enables new completion techniques depleted and fractured
                                             carbonates reservoirs.
                                          Denar Flores, Halliburton





Abstract - This paper discusses how the implementation of new technology overcame
completion difficulties in Cantarel second largest worldwide oil field. The operator requires
increasing oil production by drilling horizontal wells, but zonal isolation for gas breakthrough
and water cresting in the low pressure fractures carbonates, are a challenge and could
compromise the productivity of the well if this were not achieved.  The pay zones in Cantarel
are highly heterogeneous carbonates and dolomites, depletion of the reservoir had led
operator to abandon watered zones. Previous experience shows that isolation with traditional
techniques had not being totally successful, because the cement is loosed through the fracture
and damage the reservoir, large acid jobs are required to bring production to expected rate.
New approach to complete this well were investigated, the main goal of the technology
needed to assure zonal isolation and eliminate the use of cement on the pay zone. A packer
that uses swellable rubber to provide seal was selected to complete the well as open hole and
was able to isolate the gas cap, allowing the well to produce with lower RGA. The packer
absorb hydrocarbon to expand and make contact with the reservoir thus creating an annuli to
isolate undesirable fluids.Procedures and details of this case history are provided in this
article, focusing on the swelling elastomer technology and its capacity of achieving the seal
required. We also present the implementation of the technology in the horizontal well
Cantarel 1009-D and how the target production was reached without the need or remedial
jobs or stimulation on the pay zone.

           Deployment of Subsea Technologies
                  in Deepwater Marginal Fields
                          Christian A. Cermelli,
                        Dominique G. Roddier,
                                 Alexia Aubault.
            Marine Innovation & Technology,
                     Berkeley, California, USA.




Introduction
In recent years, an increase in exploration activities in deep and ultra-deepwater has resulted in
many oil and gas discoveries.  Very large fields holding several hundred millions of recoverable
barrels are typically large enough to justify the expenditure of a full-process facility with the
associated export infrastructure.  But most of the discoveries are too small to justify such
investment.  This trend is expected to amplify in the coming years given the number of ultra-
deepwater drilling rigs under construction or recently delivered.

When discoveries are close to an existing platform with spare production capacity, it is possible
to develop the field using subsea wellheads tied-back to the existing platform, thereby reducing
the size threshold for economic production.  Marginal fields contain significant quantities of
hydrocarbons but are not large enough for a dedicated full process platform or close enough to an
existing platform with spare process capability.  They may, however, become economic if
development costs can be reduced through novel technologies or approaches.

MARS (Multiple Application Re-injection System):
an investment in future field productivity and flexibility

Author:   Ian Donald, DES Operations Ltd, A Cameron Technology
The only thing certain in subsea oil and gas production is that at the time field
architecture design, an Operator can, at best, only estimate how a field will evolve
and develop.  In designing subsea architecture, the challenges facing Operators
today are:

    §  To maximise the NPV of assets
    §  To minimise HSE Risk
    §  To maximise incremental recovery from assets
    §  To minimise reservoir risk
    §  To minimise CAPEX
    §  To lower OPEX
    §  To maintain a flexible strategy for production optimisation
    §  To allow for low cost intervention for maintenance

The Multiple Application Re-injection System or MARS delivers this by establishing a
retrofit access port which enables any process to be fitted to any well at any time.  A
common analogy is “a USB port” for a wellhead.  Unplanned maintenance therefore
no longer requires major field shutdowns or infrastructure decommissioning; access
is simply achieved via the “USB port”. This technology delivers a low cost and flexible
field development strategy for new and existing oil fields

MARS is a production optimisation technology that establishes the wellhead as the
unit of production, enabling production optimisation systems to be mounted directly
onto Xmas trees.   The principle is simple; by introducing a coaxial flowpath insert
into the xmas tree well fluids are directed externally to a flow loop which houses a
processing technology.  The flow is returned to the wellhead and back into the
existing flowline infrastructure.  As the processing hardware is installed between the
existing isolation barriers and therefore eliminates the need for expensive, high risk
well intervention, field shut down or flowline decommissioning, whilst absolutely
minimising production losses.

Use of Swellable Elastomers to Enhance
 Cementation in Deep Water Applications

                      Bob Brooks, Tim Davis, Frank DeLucia
                                                   TAM International

Abstract


A lot of time is invested in developing a trul y integrated approach that can shorten the
planning and study timeframe while reducing uncertainties for drilling in the deepwater
arena.  Few opportunities present themselves as candidates to implement new technology
which provides assurances to these best laid plans.  One such opportunity is in the area of
cement or zonal isolation.  Swellable elastome r packers can provide assurances for zonal
isolation when primary cement jobs are difficult, or in critical areas of well construction
to ensure long term well integrity.


The deepwater environment presents numerous challenges when it comes to cementing
casing.  One such challenge is at shallow depths, low temperatures, where small
differences between pore and frac pressures require special cementing practices.  Long
openhole-highly deviated production intervals present problems with extreme
temperature and pressure changes and hole cleaning when displacing primary cement
jobs.


Too many times a poor primary cement job goes undetected by even the most advanced
cement bond evaluation tools.  Often it is only after a well is placed on production that
data suggests a lack of zonal isolation.  The cost of remedial intervention at this point is
large compared to the cost of including sw ellable packers in the initial well completion
design.

Development of a Diverless Hot Tapping System for

                                        Deep Water Pipelines

                                            Carl Henrik Ahlen
                                                    Statoil
                                           Trondheim, Norway

                                               Per Lillejordet
                                          Nemo Engineering AS
                                                Oslo, Norway

Abstract

The gas from large offshore gas fields in the North Sea and in the Norwegian Sea is
transported in long pipelines to shore for processing or transported directly to the European
market. However, marginal fields cannot carry the heavy investment cost for such long gas
transportation pipelines and must utilize the existing pipeline network infrastructure. The hot
tapping method provides cost effective tie-ins from marginal fields into existing major gas
pipelines. Hot tapping means that a new pipeline is connected to an existing pipeline in
operation with oil or gas transport at full pressure. The hot tap operation has no negative
consequences for the gas transport and gas is delivered to the market without interruption.
The method also avoids water ingress into the existing pipeline and no pigging and drying
operations are required, representing a considerable cost saving.

Statoil and other companies have used diver assisted hot tapping with a successful result. In
order to introduce the method on deep waters a diverless hot tap system is required.

As an operator of a large number of submarine pipelines Statoil and our license partners have
been responsible for the development of a Pipeline Repair System (PRS).
The PRS will be the base for the development of a Diverless Hot Tap system, DHT. The
development of DHT has been started and the system is scheduled to be ready for operation
in 2003. The PRS components that will be utilized for hot tapping will be upgraded to a
water depth of 1000 - 1500 meter.



Key Words

Pipeline, Gas Transportation, Tie in, Deep Water, Diverless Hot Tapping, Preinstalled Tee
connections, Retrofit Tee.

Light Well Intervention LWI, an important tool to achieve increased oil
                    recovery from subsea completed wells in Norwegians North Sea


                                                                                                    Authors
                                                                                  Øyvin Jensen, Statoil
                                                                              Reino T. Tryland, Statoil
                                                                                    Lars Lilledal, Statoil




Abstract
Light Well Intervention (LWI) is an important tool to achieve Statoils goal of
increasing the oil recovery from subsea completed wells in Norwegians North Sea.
On the average, the recovery factor (RF) in Statoils Subsea wells is 43% while the
goal is 55%. To achieve this target it is necessary to transfer the level of well
intervention activities performed on fixed platforms to a similar level for subsea wells.
This can only be achieved by a substantial cost reductions for these well
interventions. Statoil believe Light Well Intervention technology is one important tool
to achieve this cost reductions. By the increasing possibilities in the wire line
technology such as the well tractor development, high expandable plugs, accurate
data acquisition, high tension cables, etc. - the challenge is not the technology, but
how to reduce the cost per intervention.


This paper describes the LWI history in Statoil, a bit about the HSE & operational
performance so far, plus the way forward in terms of contracts and equipment
development

A NOVEL APPROACH TO COST EFFECTIVE SUBSEA RESERVOIR
SEABED FLUID SAMPLING METHOD
Nimi A., Fuat K., /Cranfield University

Abstract

Description

The  acquisition  of  quality  subsea  reservoir  fluid  samples           for  Green  and  Brown  field
development is crucial  for  the       correct evaluation of oil reserves and for the design of
production facilities. Due to rising operational expenditures,            operators and manufacturers
have been working hard to provide systems to enable cost effective subsea fluid sampling
solutions.

This  paper  presents  the  synergy  on        innovative  and  cutting  edge  subsea  fluid  sampling
technologies and a novel proposal on subsea sampling management.

Application

Obtaining fluid samples from actual flow stream being measured subsea is one of the
operational requirements for obtaining sustained accurate measurement for calibration of a
subsea multiphase flow meter (sMPFM). Samples collected from topside facilities do not
represent the fluid being measured. Chemical injection downstream the meter and possible
liquid separation / hold-up are typical issues. This is currently a challenge due to flow
commingling on the seabed.

Critical too is the fact that,      downhole water sample may not be collected during the
exploration  of  the    well. Hence, water sample can only be collected after the well starts
producing water. In such cases, ability to collect subsea samples may become very important.
Thus obtaining direct fluid samples measurements from the subsea tree will offer significant
benefit to the subsurface team for better reservoir performance management.

Results, Observations, Conclusions


Extensive    development  and  qualification  program  has  been  performed  by                the   subsea
industry.  Subsea     sampling     for  on-line  configuration  of     the   Multiphase    meter  to  take
measurements  of       composition     fluid  properties    in  multiphase    flow   applications    will  be
demonstrated. Methods for in line measurement of the PVT properties                   of GVF in the pipe
have been developed and qualified. A novel field application sampling strategy is developed.

Heavy vs. Light Pipe -                         An Investigation into
                                  the Lateral Response


Ayman Eltaher, PhD, PE; Aiman Al                         -showaiter, M                        Sc; Kabir Hossain, PhD, PE; Paul Jukes, PhD
                                    MCS Kenny, In c., Houston, T                       exas, USA


ABSTRACT

         A significant              research effort has been devoted lately to soil-pipe interaction during lateral
movement of a pipeline as part of addressing issues related to pipeline lateral buckling. However,
judging by the rate of development and amount of knowledge gained over this short period, it is
likely that even more is yet to be learned. One area where this statement particularl y holds is the
difference between the response of heavy and light pipes during lateral movement. Research on
cohesive soil   has   recently suggested a distinction between the two categories                                         of pipes through a
parameter that depends on the pipe weight and size and seabed soil strength. In this study, a
discussion is presented to qualify the parameter and to identify                                            possible modifications to it    that
would                 better categorize the pipe weight and determine accordingly its qualitative lateral
response. In particular, the plasticity theory and its normality condition as well as coupled
Eulerian Lagrangian finite element analyses are used to demonstrate that the ratio between the
pipe and soil weights drives more closely the pipe lateral response    for deep buried pipes. This
study provides an invaluable insight into the response of pipelines and flowlines and their
interaction           with      the seabed. For that, the study utilizes basic theoretical and state-of-the-art
numerical tools.

                      Edouard THIBAUT, Eric MEYER, Luc RIVIERE


                                TOTAL Exploration & Production




Abstract

With today’s fields fast becoming depleted and discoveries of easy-to-produce offshore oil &
gas  resources  ever  fewer,  subsea  processing  equipment  is  the  focus  of  an  extensive
development drive. The results are especially attractive for remote fields, deep waters and
tough topside environments such as Arctic locations. In order to maximize recovery of these
offshore oil & gas resources and maintain the production plateau for as long as possible,
subsea  compression  and  subsea  boosting  are  more  and  more            frequently   required.   This
generates  the  need  to  develop     highly  reliable  subsea    electrical  power   transmission    and
distribution systems, for deployment over long step-outs and in deep waters.

This paper proposes      two  innovative   electrical architectures    for sea-floor  compression and
pumping applications based on       AC transmission and distribution schemes. It also addresses
the constraints of the    offshore oil & gas environment and presents           the key functions of a
subsea electrical transmission and distribution system.

Summary
A substantial number of risers have been constructed by Heerema Marine Contractors (HMC)
for floaters such as SPAR’s, TLP’s and Semi’s in the Gulf of Mexico. The majority of HMC
experience involved the (Pipe in Pipe) Steel Catenary Riser (SCR) type. Over the years the
need for  alternatives  to SCR and Flexibles     has increased   given especially the requirements
for a larger number of risers in deeper       water and congested field environments.        This has
resulted in concepts such as the integrally     installed Hybrid Riser tower, Single Line Offset
Riser (SLOR) and Tension Leg Riser (TLR). Most recently HMC has delivered (EPCI) nine
SLOR type Risers on Angola Block 31.

Together with TOTAL and INTECSEA, HMC is developing a new riser system which
increases the available suite of deepwater riser solutions. It is an offshore constructed hybrid
riser bundle installed using Heavy Lift and        Pipe  Lay vessels. An evaluation qualification
program has been run under the direction of TOTAL to ensure that all major uncertainties
(Maturity and Risk) are manageable within the design evolution to ensure compliance in its
application on future deepwater development opportunities.

This paper will give an overview of available riser systems in deeper water for a congested
field lay-out, present the novel solution as well as results from the associated development
program.

Extending the operational envelope of
  production risers to unprecedented water
     depths: Thermoplastic Composite Riser

     Jens de Kanter and Martin van Onna -
                Airborne Composite Tubulars


Abstract
As more oil fields are found offshore, the requirement for offshore production risers
increases. In addition, these new reservoirs are found in increasingly deep waters (over 2500
metres). Currently, steel catenary risers (SCR) and flexible pipes are used for the application
of production risers. SCR are limited in their operational envelope in terms of maximum
water depth due to the strength to weight ratio. In addition, they have limitations in catenary
configuration in shallow and medium water depth with larger diameters, due to their high
stiffness and large Minimum Bending Radius (MBR). Flexible pipes have small MBR and
proven track-record, but are expensive, complex and have a limited operational envelope.

This paper will describe the concept of a Thermoplastic Composite Riser (TCR) and put it
into perspective with respect to conventional flexibles and SCR. The composite system is
based on melt-fusing multiple Fibre-Reinforced thermoplastic tapes on a thermoplastic pipe
of the same base material. The result is a lightweight, ultra high strength and fatigue resistant
riser system.

Introduction
Currently the oil and gas industry is developing its operations into increasingly difficult
reservoirs, where they stretch the capabilities of conventional technologies. One of the major
elements is going deeper, over 2500 meters. Here the increase in weight for steel pipes is very
severe, which has a big impact on the riser design (e.g. incorporating expensive buoyancy)
and on the installation and operation.

Internal Weld Scanning


                                       Dr. Tim Clarke
                                  Dr. Richard Gooch

                   Optical Metrology Services Ltd


 1    Abstract

This paper addresses the up and coming needs of projects to ensure that weld root profiles are
within specification. The context of the requirement is outlined for such applications as
internally coated pipe, CRA clad pipes, carbon steel pipes and manifolds. A new service has
been introduced into the market which addresses all of the stringent requirements of the
industry. The operation of the weld scanning tool is described in this paper and the way in
which it is applied is discussed in different project settings.

 2    Introduction

There are a number of reasons why scanning the region of the weld is required:

 2.1    To ensure internal coatings are applied correctly
For pipes that are internally coated it is required that the cut back area in the region of the weld
must be coated before the pipes are lowered into the sea from a lay barge. Tools exist which
are capable of shot blasting the weld area and applying coating material in this region several
stations down the firing line. An example of such a system is the one offered by CRTS in their
coating service. The application of a coating is subject to certain constraints. Any feature of the
weld which is sharp or projects above a certain height could cause a coating flaw at that point.

Prepare the Unknown – The new paradigm
                       for operating underwater


                                 Olivier Kleindienst / Manfred Lueth
                                 KOLPI, Sophia Antipolis, FRANCE

Abstract.   We  present  a  new  human  system  interface  and  its  underlying  concept  to
understand the impact of volumetric perception on discovery and navigation. We will
give a historical dimension of the development, starting with Prince Albert I (1847-
1922). Followed, by a review of the technologies reconstructing the distant situation and
the  limitations  for  operating  today.  Finally,  we  will  show  first  results  from  tests
performed with IFREMER as well as present the latest technology developments and its
impact for deepwater applications.


                                             INTRODUCTION

A. Towards the next discovery
 While the surface of the earth is rather well known, the subsurface of the oceans remains
relatively unknown.  The volume of the oceans is of around 1.3 billion cubic kilometres.
Scientists, corporations and States are engaged in exploring this immense volume, hoping to
discover and learn from it as well as protect it, but also to extract from it and exploit it.  All
start, prior to exploitation, with surveying and exploring the area concerned.


B. Prince Albert I, pioneer in oceanography
 One of the early explorers in oceanography was Prince Albert I., the great-great-grandfather
of  the  current  Sovereign  Prince  Albert  of  Monaco.  There  are  at  least  three  reasons  to
recognize his merits related to the theme of this conference and this presentation. First, he was
not only an active explorer but also a smart inventor contributing several inventions to the
progress of science. Secondly, he is also known to be a user of daguerreotype, the precursor
technology  for  modern  photography  and  last  but  not  least,  he  founded  the  famous
Oceanographic Institute in Monaco.


C. Problem to prepare for the “Unknown”
 Today, mankind has three methods available for exploring the underwater world, the two
best-known methods being submarine travel or diving. The third and the only one available
for deepwater is an indirect method involving the use of unmanned vehicles.

DOT 2009 - Shell Perdido - Installation of the World's Deepest SPAR
René de Koeijer, Olaf Willemse, Ewout Voors (Heerema Marine Contractors)

Summary
Heerema Marine Contractors (HMC) was awarded the installation several key components
of Shell‟s Perdido Development. Under two separate contracts, HMC was to install the
flowlines, Steel Catenary Risers (SCRs), subsea structures and SPAR platform. The project
contained a number of record installations for both deep water and topside installation. i.e.
the deepest SPAR ever, deepest permanent suction piles, deepest ever flowlines and pipeline
end structure and an integrated topsides installation new US Gulf of Mexico record lift
weight.

This paper addresses the various challenges Heerema Marine Contractors had to address. It
also highlights the organizational capabilities required to; integrate the teams working on the
project, making sure that hurricane preparedness is in place, create flexibility in installation
sequences and schedule of the various components to be installed during the installation
campaign and support this with the necessary procedures, optimizing vessel workability and
supporting logistics.

All these items paid off during the 2008 installation campaign when the project was faced to
deal with 3 major hurricanes with a flexible schedule window for the SPAR installation
within the other activities in that campaign.

Design Options for Lightweight Deep Water
                                        Drilling Risers


                              Harry R. Zonker, Matthew P. Kiley, Alcoa Inc.
                             Michael D. Ritchie, David Walters, 2H Offshore



ABSTRACT
Oil operators continue to be faced with escalating costs to drill and complete wells in deep
waters.  This is due, in part, to a limited number of available drilling vessels which have a
sufficient water depth rating.  The limited number of vessels along with increased demand has
continued to push drilling day rates to higher levels, exceeding $500,000 USD per day in some
cases.  To meet the demand for deeper water drilling vessels, drilling contractors must either
build new or upgrade older vessels to accommodate the increased water depth.  Both of these
options can be time and cost prohibitive.  An alternative option for drillers is the use of a lighter
weight riser system which can extend the water depth rating of an existing rig with minimal to no
modification of its structure.  The focus of this paper is the development of advanced aluminum-
based design solutions to enable drillers to ach ieve a lighter weight riser system.  One solution
reviewed is retro-fitting auxiliary lines on current steel risers with advanced alloys.  Steel
auxiliary lines can represent as much as 50% of the total assembled riser joint weight, thus
present a significant riser system weight savi ngs opportunity.  A more holistic solution, also
detailed in this paper, is a new lightweight drilling riser design.  The new design incorporates
advanced alloys and alternative manufacturing methods which result in improved performance
over traditional welded aluminum designs.  Specifically, strength improvements of 25% are
achieved while providing increased corrosion resistance and improved inspection.  Also, the
inherent stiffness of the aluminum-based system offers potential improvements in VIV fatigue
performance.  The new lightweight riser system design solutions are shown to be a cost effective
alternative for extending the water depth rati ng of existing rigs by providing sufficient deep
water riser length, while staying within the vessels’ structural support, tensioner, draw-works and
variable deck loading capacities.

Installation Analysis of Spar Top Tensioned Risers

                Hengliang (Henry) Yuan, Xiaohua Lu, and Roger Burke

                                                    Technip

ABSTRACT

Spar top tensioned risers have provided a dry-tree solution to numerous deep-water applications
in the Gulf of Mexico and         offshore Malaysia. These risers are typically a centralized vertical
multi-tube system, consisting of        a production tubing inside a single or dual-casing            riser string,
which is supported by either buoyancy cans or by the Spar through hydro-pneumatic tensioners.
Riser installation requires careful analysis, planning and execution to assure correct in-service
tension distribution and riser stroke.

This paper presents an enhanced installation analysis methodology for Spar top tensioned risers.
The  method  is  generic,  applicable  to  both  buoyancy  can  and             Spar   supported  vertical  riser
(SSVR) systems. An uncoupled analysis that treats the riser only is used for the buoyancy can
risers and a coupled analysis that includes both the riser and the Spar hull is used for the SSVR.
The complete analysis can be programmed in a single Excel workbook.                        Requiring minimum
input, this Excel-based installation analysis can be conveniently performed in the field.

The correct in-service tension distribution among riser strings is obtained by adjusting the stretch
of each riser string during installation. The amount of stretch applied to each riser string during
installation is back-calculated from the tension at the normal in-service condition, accounting for
the effects of riser contents, annulus pressure, and temperature variations. Riser stroke at each
step of installation is determined through back-calculation of the normal in-service riser stroke.
Installation parameters are calculated for both the buoyancy can riser and SSVR systems, and
their differences are discussed.

                                             ABSTRACT

The Offshore industry has had to foster innovation in order to face the world’s most
challenging environments. But, innovation has not always been synonymous with industry
wide acceptance. The introduction of the Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) only came
about as the industry understood the possibilities that the new technology delivered. Through
the years the spectrum of ROV tasks has steadily grown and today it is the workhorse of
Subsea operations. But, the industry must now face new challenges as its rapid expansion into
deeper water and harsher environments pushes resources and current technology to the limit.
To meet this challenge new concepts of operations and novel solutions are required. Taking a
leaf from the history of the ROV this paper will present a new Autonomous Vehicle concept
that will lead the way to new services and opportunities. This concept is the result of a
programme of work that has been partly sponsored to date by BP and Chevron. These oil
majors have understood the possibilities and are working in collaboration with SeeByte and
Subsea 7 to deliver a new service to the offshore industry. The presentation will provide the
delegates with a picture of how the technology will be used and show the latest results that
demonstrate how close the technology is to being delivered.

Title:
Safer Bend Stiffener Connections for Flexible Risers and Umbilicals on Deepwater Platforms

Authors:

Paul Hughes, Business Development Manager, First Subsea Ltd.

Steven Bray, Engineered Products Sales Manager, Trelleborg CRP Ltd,

Abstract:

As operators move into frontier fields so they need flexible riser and umbilical connection
technology that reflects the rigorous demands of this offshore, deepwater environment. Recent
developments in bend stiffener connection technology have focused on improving the speed,
reliability and safety of installing riser and umbilical connections.


Bend stiffeners are a common sight on many deepwater platforms where they are used to reduce
wear and fatigue in flexible risers and umbilicals.  Installing bend stiffeners, however, can be a time
consuming and hazardous business, especially where divers are involved. This paper reports on
research into diverless bend stiffener connectors that are safer and easier to install, using a ball and
taper connector for a diverless connection.


The paper will also cover developments in diverless bend stiffener connector technology
specifically designed to meet the meteorological conditions of the Gulf of Mexico. Here a flexible
connection is possible allowing risers and umbilicals to be disconnected quickly and simply using
an ROV, should the production platform need to be moved in the event of severe weather
conditions.


In addition, the paper will examine the mechanical engineering challenges faced when developing
diverless connection systems that can be used either with existing platform's I / J tubes with or
without bellmouths. Further work on this diverless connector system has led to the development of
compact ball and taper designs for connections where space and access is limited.

Light Well Intervention LWI, an important tool to achieve increased oil
                    recovery from subsea completed wells in Norwegians North Sea


                                                                                                    Authors
                                                                                  Øyvin Jensen, Statoil
                                                                              Reino T. Tryland, Statoil
                                                                                    Lars Lilledal, Statoil




Abstract
Light Well Intervention (LWI) is an important tool to achieve Statoils goal of
increasing the oil recovery from subsea completed wells in Norwegians North Sea.
On the average, the recovery factor (RF) in Statoils Subsea wells is 43% while the
goal is 55%. To achieve this target it is necessary to transfer the level of well
intervention activities performed on fixed platforms to a similar level for subsea wells.
This can only be achieved by a substantial cost reductions for these well
interventions. Statoil believe Light Well Intervention technology is one important tool
to achieve this cost reductions. By the increasing possibilities in the wire line
technology such as the well tractor development, high expandable plugs, accurate
data acquisition, high tension cables, etc. - the challenge is not the technology, but
how to reduce the cost per intervention.


This paper describes the LWI history in Statoil, a bit about the HSE & operational
performance so far, plus the way forward in terms of contracts and equipment
development

Abstract

For new build FPSOs or to safely extend the life of ageing assets, operators require technologies that enable them
to safely monitor the subsea infrastructure in real-time, to identify problems before they occur. Annual inspections
by Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV)                   although useful to provide close up                inspection, do not provide real-time
information in the event of a mooring line failure or problem with the risers.

Through the application of multibeam sonar technology, operators can now have real-time 24/7 information on the
presence and position of mooring chains, risers and umbilicals. Unlike other acoustic techniques, multibeam sonar
does not require additional sensors mounted to each mooring chain or riser, therefore removing the need for
regular maintenance, servicing and power source replacement by ROVs.

The multibeam sonar system provides autonomous alarms in the event of mooring line or bend stiffener failure and
the accurate sonar data can be used for further fatigue analysis, assisting in the planned maintenance schedule.

This unique technology was developed for BP and has been successfully deployed on an FPSO in the North Sea,
where it has provided round-the-clock integrity monitoring capability. This                           technology      was selected in 2013 for
permanent deployment on a new build FPSO entering service in the North Sea with production planned for 2015.

Introduction

Over the past decade, a number of studies and Joint Industry Projects (JIP) have been carried out to investigate
how to improve and better manage the integrity of moorings and riser systems used by FPSOs. As highlighted in a
number of these reports, given the safety critical nature of mooring lines and the consequences of a ruptured riser,
one might imagine that they would be heavily instrumented with automated alarms which would be activated in the
case of failure. In practice many FPSOs are not equipped with such instrumentation or alarms. This is often due to
a lack of consensus in regulation, or lack of understanding of how best to address the problem. For example, how
does an operator distinguish between mooring line failure and instrumentation failure without direct intervention, for
turrets where the mooring chains are permanently locked off under the hull?

The main form of monitoring continues to be General Visual Inspection (GVI) by ROV which is performed by all
operators, most commonly on an annual basis. The main limitation with annual GVI is that it is only a snapshot and
where it detects failure, it is after the event. GVI also has a number of other limitations that include;

         Environmental restrictions – inspection is dependent upon suitable environmental operating conditions
         Difficult to identify small areas of damage
         Difficult or impractical to operate in a confined or enclosed space
         Requires ROV support or Diver Support Vessel (DSV) with associated costs
         Marine growth often masks damage

Power Delivery and Umbilical Cable
      Optimisation for Long Offset Tiebacks

                       1                     1                 1                2                     2
        Paul Overton    , Daniel Denning      , Neil Douglas    , Daniel Byrd    , Rory Mackenzie
                          1 Viper Subsea LLP, Portishead, United Kingdom
                                 2 Total SA, 64018 Pau Cedex, France

Abstract

In this paper we present a study into the physical and practical limitations of different power
transmission  techniques  for  long  offset  tiebacks.    The  results  from  the  study  present  a
definitive operating envelope       for varying offset tiebacks and subsea power demands.                 The
study is supported by in-depth performance analyses covering a range of power transmission
techniques and umbilical cable designs.  We also include the economic considerations when
evaluating the different power delivery and umbilical cable selections.

1    Introduction
Over the past 10 years there have been a number of examples of subsea field developments
where the tieback distance has been defined as 'long offset', typically with the flow-line and
umbilical lengths being over 70km and up to 150km.
   To date, the electrical power transmission techniques and umbilical designs have simply
been 'extensions' of the technology used for more conventional 'short offset' developments.
There is a trend for ever increasing offset distances and higher power demands from subsea
consumers, typically subsea processing equipment.  The higher power levels and increasing
offsets means that there is now more focus on power delivery capacities as well as the
installed umbilical costs.
   Extensive work has been undertaken to re-evaluate the physical and practical limitations of
different  power  transmission  techniques  and  to  assess  the  impact  of  different  umbilical
designs on these limitations.
   This   study  supported  by  in-depth  performance  analyses  covering  a  range  of  power
transmission  techniques,  umbilical  cable  designs  has  resulted  in  a  family  of  definitive
operating envelopes.  Economic evaluations of the different solutions considered Operational
Expenditure (OPEX), Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) and installation costs to ensure that full
technical and commercial comparisons could be made for a wide range of field development
scenarios.

2    Subsea Electrical Distribution Architectures
Within the Subsea Oil and Gas Production Control System (PCS) sector, a variety of system
electrical distribution architectures are used, ranging from the simple ‘bus-bar’                   Electrical
Distribution Unit (EDU)       based systems, to transformer based EDUs and the more complex
systems incorporating Subsea Router Module (SRM) technology to enable communications
distribution and active power monitoring and switching.
   In spite of the variety of system architectures, the majority of these systems utilise single
phase AC, 50/60Hz or DC at voltages up to 1.2kV for the power transmission across the main
umbilical.  There are of course a few exceptions to this that include three phase at up to 3kV.

Abstract

The  area of subsea developments has today a strong emphasis in the oil                 & gas industry, with subsea
boosting being the most mature area relating to subsea processing. However with the development
and qualifications done for separation        technologies, it is possible today to increase the value of
subsea processing solutions including separation. This            can reduce the need for hydrate inhibition,
reduce power requirements, simplify the topsides design to mention a few examples.                    For deepwater
solutions, there are fewer     separation   solution alternatives, which will be either compact          inline type of
equipment or of spherical design.

Introduction

ASCOM Separation has over the recent years developed and supplied high performance compact
technologies for    gas/liquid separation,     oil/water separation,     de-sanding and      de-oiling. The
technologies have     been tested and verified both for topsides as well as for performing subsea
processing qualification and is part of continued development and applications.                  The subsea
qualifications have taken place at a realistic conditions multiphase             flowloop with high flow capacity
(up to 50.000 BLPD)     at pressures up to 45 barg, run for crude oils in the API range of 19 to             36.

In the recent years,    there have been some subsea developments including separation                     at the seabed,
mostly with gas/liquid separation, but also with oil/water separation                    as well as produced water
treatment.    The level of   technology     development and advances in           wellstream    separation    has shown
that subsea separation is feasible.

More frequently, multiphase boosting solutions are used,               allowing   the full wellstream to be pumped
in the multiphase units, without any separation equipment. This                   has required a lot of technology
development for      complex    rotary  mechanical equipment         and requiring a different field infrastructure
than if separation    would    be part of the solution. The multiphase boosting is not             necessarily   the best
solution, as will be described later in this paper, as separation can            introduce    further benefits used as
part of the boosting solution, for both greenfield as well as brownfield developments.

Emulsion/Sludge-Induced Slugging in Subsea
                                               Tieback
     L. Wang, L. A. Dykhno, G. J. Zabaras and Z. Huo, Shell Global Solutions (US) Inc.
  C. R. Holloway, N. B. Dee and W. Nisbet JR, Shell Exploration & Production Company


Abstract
A  Shell subsea tieback in GoM           has experienced numerous production              issues such as wax,
asphaltenes, scale, emulsions and sand production. In addition to various flow assurance issues,
slugging was also observed after well stimulation jobs. The observed slugging was characterized
by high pressure fluctuations and significant water cut variations              which lead to platform trips.
The slugging combined with other flow assurance issues made the slugging behavior difficult to
distinguish    and  understand  from        the   multiphase  flow  perspective         and    to  mitigate  this
phenomenon.

The primary purpose of the study was to identify the root cause of the observed slugging patterns
via transient multiphase flow simulations. Several mechanisms which could provide reasonable
explanation for the     slugging behavior have been proposed and investigated.                 In particular, the
mechanisms  of  riser-induced  severe  slugging,  terrain-induced             slugging,  growing  slugs,  and
unstable  oscillating     flow  were  studied.  Other  possible  explanations  related  to  flowline
topography,  organic  solid  deposition  and  emulsion/sludge  have  also  been  investigated.
Comparisons between the simulation results and the field data allowed the validation of various
slugging mechanisms,        identify the most probable root cause of the slugging               and recommend
mitigation strategies.

A flow map was developed through transient simulations to identify the slugging boundaries and
validate the proposed slugging mechanisms. The flow map indicates that the observed slugging
pattern in the field is not expected from a traditional modeling perspective. Further investigation
has shown that the mechanism of emulsion/sludge-induced slugging is quite valid in explaining
the behavior and this hypothesis is supported by the known field conditions and observations.
The  emulsion/sludge  may  be  generated  from  subsea  choking  or                fluid  incompatibility  from
different wells.   Further validation of this       hypothesis    can be performed once         a liquid   sample
during normal production is available. The mitigation strategy proposed is to produce compatible
wells as much as possible with fully open topsides choke.

Managing the Impact of Obsolescence on Subsea Field Development in
                                     the Deep Offshore Industry
                               Abili N, Citi G, Eni E&P; Onwuzuluigbo R, Saipem
                      Deep Offshore Technology International Conference, October 22 – 24, 2013.

Abstract

The  current  deep  offshore  trend       (DOT)    presents  new     oil  and  gas  discovery  opportunities  with
commercial quantities. This has resulted in new              architectures and      technology developments on
subsea hardwares, FPSO or Platform construction and new control systems to meet the challenges
associated with these emerging deepwater field developments.

The  overall  impact     of  revolutionizing     subsea    technology  developments  is  that  legacy  system
becomes  obsolete  and  proves  challenging  for  ageing  fields.  This  is a  significant  problem  facing
offshore Operators as many are discovering that they are unable to execute like-to-like replacement
of failed equipment as they are no longer supported in the market. This poses a very serious
challenge to system availability during component or equipment failure. Shut-in-time is extended
which implies loss of production and in some extreme cases, resulting in complete failure of asset.

Therefore, this have necessitated the need for obsolescence solutions to enable the integration of
legacy systems with future proof systems in realising value of assets and thus reduce the occurrence
of obsolescence or its impact on subsea production facilities.

The present paper focuses on the strategy to implement life cycle obsolescence management to
bridge the gaps on existing brown field development and future proof green field development in
the deep offshore industry.

Subsea Installation in Extreme Water Depths
                            – A Contractor’s View

       Kees van Zandwijk, Radboud van Dijk,
                                    Eelco Harmsen,
               Heerema Marine Contractors SE


ABSTRACT
Deepwater lowering has seen a rapid development over the past 20 years. From the first
foundation piles of Tension Leg Platforms in 1000m water depth, via the installation of heavy
anchor piles in 2000 to 3000m of water, the industry is now at the brink of lowering heavy and
sizable subsea production units into deep and ultra-deep water.

When investing in Deep Water Lowering equipment, the discussion circles around the choice for
steel wires or fiber ropes. These two cannot easily be exchanged with the aim to test the new
technology of fiber ropes or to simply use the best of both in the given situation. As steel wires
and fiber ropes require totally different systems that mutually exclude each other, the choice has
the nature of an either-or decision.

This either-or decision is further complicated by the fact that the dynamic behavior of Deep
Water Lowering systems strongly depends on the vessel from which it is operated; on the water
depths in which it is deployed; and on the wave climate in which the operation takes place.
Moreover, small and slender structures behave totally differently as compared to large and heavy
ones when lowered to the seabed.

The paper presents a short reconnaissance study of landing different types of structures on the
seabed, assessing the operability of different types of installation vessels when using steel wires
and fiber ropes. Offshore Support Vessels appear to have an acceptable operability only when
fiber ropes are used in combination with Active Heave Compensation. A semisubmersible crane
vessel in general does better using steel wires. Only in ultra-deep water of 3000m do fiber ropes
usually perform better. The application of an elastic stretcher in the lifting arrangement may have
the same effect as a step from steel wires to fiber ropes and is a subject worth further
investigation.

Combining High Fidelity Nonlinear Simulations
         with DNV Methodologies for Enhanced
                Dropped Objects Risk Assessment

Arya Majed1, Peter Brownlie2, and Phil Cooper3
                                          INTECSEA



Abstract

Accidentally dropped objects pose a serious and costly hazard to subsea installations. The DNV
provides coarse guidelines, based on an object’s shape and weight, which sets the variance on the
assumed normal distribution for the object’s scatter pattern. However, these guidelines are based
on simplified assumptions which do not incorporate the object’s complex geometry and the
influence of various glide and drag features on hydrodynamics and resulting                    impact on the
excursions. In this paper,     3D   nonlinear simulations are utilized to accurately predict the fall
trajectories of objects with complex geometries. The resulting high fidelity scatter pattern can
then be incorporated in the DNV dropped object damage risk assessment, in place of the DNV
default probability distribution, resulting in a far more realistic damage risk assessment.

The methodology presented in this paper is a significant advancement in efficient 3D nonlinear
simulation of dropped objects allowing for quick determination of trajectories even for deep
water  applications.  The  objects  analyzed  may  be  complex  in  geometry  since  the  method
discretizes the object via a large number of drag nodes. The fast execution speeds allow for the
object’s initial orientation angles, a key determinant of the trajectory and impact location, to be
randomized in a vast suite of Monte-Carlo simulations thus determining the entire impact zone.
The   object’s   large   rotations   and   translations   coupled   with   its   orientation   dependent
hydrodynamics are efficiently and accurately simulated as the object falls through water.

The subject method constitutes a significant advancement over existing commercial software
capabilities which require prohibitively long computational times for just a few hundred feet of
drop. The method is utilized to simulate the trajectories for          a manifold down to 7000 feet and
determine the entire impact zone. The manifold trajectories are post-processed to determine the
excursion statistics and probability distribution.       These results are then compared to the DNV
predicted scatter pattern for this category of object.          Significant discrepancies are identified,

Pull or No-pull:
Risk-based Decision Support for Subsea Blowout Preventers (BOPs)

Scotty Roper, Commercial Manager, Lloyd’s Register Energy – Drilling

Overview

The tragic Gulf of Mexico accident in April, 2010 can be marked as the defining moment which confirmed the idea
for making a subsea Blowout Preventer (BOP) risk model.

The accident showed that society is our biggest stakeholder with its own risk acceptance perception, enabled by the
immediacy  of     social-media,  the     tenacity  of  the   press,  and  today’s  instantaneous  technology  for  transmitting
newsworthy and life-altering events.

When thinking back to that day in April, we can ask: what does the majority of society remember                               about   this
tragedy? The most common answer to this question is the graphic photos of massive amounts of oil washing up on
once pristine Gulf beaches, killing fish, birds, and other ancillary industries which rely on clean Gulf waters and
beaches to survive. Although not pictured with such detail, the casualties will never be forgotten either.

Why create a risk model? Society created the need

Societal risk awareness and its        acceptance or non-acceptance          have created the need to continually improve the
management of drilling-related risks, and thus created the demand for better decision making tools. But there were
industry-wide inherent difficulties:
          • The industry was faced with a very conservative approach to BOP component failure
          • This conservatism was fed by the fear that something could go badly, but was also very costly to prevent

The decision of whether or not to pull a subsea Blowout Preventer after identification of a BOP component failure is
very delicate, and involves many critical risk factors.

Some of the inherent problems run into included:
          • BOP pulling is costly and time-consuming: major Non-Productive Time (NPT)
          • BOP pulling is an extreme risk in itself

Title:  Simulations, or Wet SITs, As Risk Reduction for Sea Trials:
When There Is Only One Chance To Safely Do It Right

400 word-limited abstract:

In the interest of safety, risk reduction, and operational excellence, NASA uses the Neutral Buoyancy
Laboratory (NBL) to simulate complex space operations, working out procedures and timelines in a
controlled, underwater environment, before the operation is executed in the harsh environment of
space.   This extensive underwater operations expertise and safety culture is being leveraged by
companies in the energy industry to develop and trouble-shoot operations and procedures for use of new
technologies in subsea tools and equipment, including:

•Sensors, advanced imaging and scanning devices using Radiographic, Electromagnetic Acoustic, and
other technologies

•Integration of ROVs, AUVs, and ADSs with custom test tools

•Repair and inspection methodologies

•Simulation of high risk interventions

There have been several testing successes using NBL as an intermediate step toward sea trials for new
technologies and new methodologies, increasing the safety and lowering the risk of the operation in open
water.  Recent customers have commented that no other facility has all the capabilities needed in one
place like the NBL, making wet SIT and timeline development for new technology efficient and productive.

Simulation in the NBL is a proven method for developing and verifying procedures and timelines for
complex operations before moving to an extremely hazardous environment.  This intermediate step will
significantly lower risk and increase reliability, while enhancing project execution, management, and
safety by ensuring operational readiness prior to moving to the deepwater environment.  Simulations and
Wet SITs in this controlled environment increase the availability and productivity of critical resources in
the Houston area while they test solutions to problems before going offshore.

Wet SITs increase simulation and training fidelity by utilizing an actual underwater environment, with full
use of control systems, including thrust, buoyancy, added mass, attached tool behavior, and overall
system response.  The lessons-learned from previous efforts were that computer simulations were
sometimes too idealistic, buoyancy control challenges were underestimated, and attached tool behavior
was not accurately predicted in early design revisions.  Procedures and designs were modified during
simulations in the NBL, prior to offshore implementation, saving significant time and effort in the more
expensive, less forgiving offshore environment.

•Riser Chain Repair SIT in 2011 – Included proof of concept for inspection technology, test jig
prototyping, simulation verification, and repair methodologies development.

Abstract
The ability to maintain stationkeeping throughout severe environmental loading is critical to the
safe operations of permanently moored floating facilities. Failures of forged mooring
components have been observed on these facilities and noted by the issuance of multiple safety
notices by United States regulatory bodies (U.S. Department of the Interior Safety Alerts No.
259 on 16 January 2008 and No. 296 on 12 May 2011). These alerts highlighted the need for

toughness values, which will be demonstrated in this paper. Given the potential existence of the

summarized in this paper which can be employed within operators’ integrity management

Introduction

The  transition  from  design  to  getting  assets,  built,  installed,  commissioned and  handed  over to
operations is a complex and largely schedule driven process.  There are a variety of competing
demands, and even where the same drivers are focussing             people’s minds they can end up with very
different and conflicting ways of achieving the same aim.  Often the process is managed in a very silo
based arrangement and this is recognised by the creation of a position such as an interface manager to
try and bridge the gaps.  Integrity Management is a discipline that works best when a system approach
is applied and this is often something that is at odds with the silos that occur in a project environment.

Many projects have some kind of lessons learned review at some point either during or post project
completion.  These can be a valuable source of information for similar projects or the next phase of
the  ongoing  project,  but    perhaps  these  lessons  are  not     typically   being   effectively  utilised   and
communicated.  When it comes to the ultimate result of a major accident event, this failure to learn is
something    the  National  Offshore  Petroleum  Safety  and  Environmental  Management  Authority
(NOPSEMA),       recently cited as a problem.        They   highlighted that companies are saving time and
money in the design stage, at the expense of good risk management.  Risk management underpins
integrity management and, therefore, good risk management is good integrity management.

This paper discusses some of the things that need to be thought about when applying integrity
management within a project lifecycle.

These all help to get the point across that integrity management is whole of life, not just an operations
phase activity, and is made up of an integrated suite of activities, not just an inspection plan, not just

                                                www.nov.com

ABSTRACT
The fatigue design of the steel armour layers is an important factor in flexible riser design.
Typically, the riser must be able to endure the loads of a field condition for a period of 20
years.  In  flexible  pipe  design,  this  is  analysed  in  global  and  local  flexible  pipe  fatigue
modelling.  However,        modelling     needs  to  be  supported  by  proper  testing.  One  of  the
widespread test methods is the so-called in-plane bending fatigue testing which is one of the
important qualification tests for flexible pipes. In spite of this, literature contains only limited
guidance about the test procedures. Some guidance is found in API 17B/ ISO 13628-11. It is
the aim of the present paper to provide more specific guidance on the selection of test
parameters. A result of the review of the test parameters is a clear picture of the coverage of a
specific test. This is important when judging whether a new in                  plane test is required for a
specific  pipe    /  project.  Since  there  is  no  unique  relation  between  field  data  and  test
parameters,    one  test  programme  will  cover  different  fields  and  vice  versa.  In  order  to
intelligently transfer the knowledge obtained in one test to different pipe designs and different
fields  it  is  necessary  to  understand  the  steps  in  the  fatigue  model,  and  these  steps  are
schematized here-in.      The focus     is on the calculation     of armour wire stress. NOV           Flexibles
has, over the past 12 years, built up knowledge on the              modelling of the real strain response
during cyclic bending and tension. This has been done using fibre bragg gratings embedded in
the tensile armour layers. In this work it has been shown that NOV Flexibles is able to model
the tensile armour stresses at low and high angles which is necessary to conclude from test to
different field applications. The conclusions drawn in the paper are supported by examples
from actual fatigue testing.

ABSTRACT
For a number of years, the creep performance of standard High Modulus Polyethylene (HMPE) fiber
types has limited their use in synthetic offshore mooring systems. In 2003, a low creep HMPE fiber was
introduced and qualified for semi-permanent MODU moorings.
This paper reports on a new High Modulus Polyethylene fiber type with significantly improved creep
properties compared to other HMPE fiber types, which, for the first time, allows its use in permanent
offshore mooring systems, for example for deepwater FPSO moorings.
Results on fiber and rope creep experiments and stiffness measurements are reported. Laboratory
testing shows that ropes made with the new fiber type retain the properties characteristic of HMPE such
as high static strength and stiffness, and high tension fatigue resistance.


INTRODUCTION
With oil and gas field exploration going deeper and further offshore, mooring system designers are
faced with engineering mooring systems that balance the demands of maximum platform offsets, wind
and wave peak loads, and long-term high tensions in loop currents.
Polyester ropes are commonly used for deepwater moorings. Beyond 2,000m water depth, however,
the high stretch of the polyester rope becomes a problem as the longer mooring lines allow greater
horizontal offsets. A 2,000m polyester line may have 40m elongation, while a 3,000m line would allow
60m elongation under the same environmental conditions, creating greater horizontal offsets which
may exceed the limits of risers. Using High Modulus Polyethylene with similar break load these offsets
would be only 12m for a 3,000m line.
At the same time polyester ropes require large vessels for transport and installation. Especially outside
of the GOM these are not readily available and if available need to planned a long time before their
potential use. Operators therefor are looking for mooring systems that can be transported and installed
from smaller and more readily available vessels.

ABSTRACT
This  paper   demonstrates the importance of having            ready  a  mooring integrity management
plan, including a mooring failure rapid response plan, to ensure that potential anomalies on a
moored FPSO can be addressed quickly with minimum impact on production. An overview of
a typical mooring integrity management plan              that  includes the sparing strategy,       mooring
replacement procedures and plans for mobilisation of construction vessels                  is presented for
FPSO spread mooring and turret mooring systems.               Two major components of the mooring
failure rapid response plan,      the assessment of the mooring system residual capacity after
mooring leg    failure and the development of the mooring line replacement procedures, are
illustrated using two examples. The mooring residual capacity study, undertaken for a generic
FPSO with a disconnectable turret mooring system operated in the North West Shelf                           of
Western Australia, has been used as an example. This paper shows the methodology and main
results from   the advanced mooring analysis used to determine the residual capacity of the
mooring system and the associated limiting weather conditions, which may be used when
deciding whether FPSO can safely continue to operate after the loss of one mooring line until
permanent  repairs      are  carried  out.   An  example  of  generic         mooring  line  replacement
procedures    is  shown    for  a  spread-moored  FPSO  in         1000    metres   water  depth.    Typical
methodology of replacing the mooring leg, including a suction pile and a long wire rope, is
presented. The paper concludes that preparedness of an FPSO operator, prior modelling and
analysis of the mooring and riser systems and availability of up-to-date analytical models are
essential for the rapid response activities to be efficiently undertaken after a mooring failure.

Mooring  system  of      floating  production  storage  and  offloading         facility (FPSO)  provides
station  keeping    for   the  asset   during  production,     maintaining  vessel      excursions  within
allowable   limits  for  the  operation of risers and hydrocarbons offloading            under anticipated
metocean conditions.
There   are  two  main  types  of  FPSO  mooring  systems—permanently  connected                          and
disconnectable—used for different types of metocean conditions. Permanent mooring systems
are typically   designed for    FPSOs staying on station         in non-cyclonic environments         for the
duration of its design life     (for example,     in  West Africa,      South-East    Asia  or North Sea).
Disconnectable mooring systems are typically used for cyclonic environmental conditions (for
example,   in  Western    Australia‘s   North   West Shelf) and allow quick          disconnection of the
FPSO from the mooring system to evade cyclones. Disconnectable mooring systems are also
used for FPSOs in Arctic areas to avoid ultimate ice loads or collision with icebergs.
The majority of permanently connected FPSOs in benign environments have spread mooring
systems,   typically   made  up  of  four  line  clusters,  each  containing  several  mooring  legs.
Permanently moored FPSOs, in harsh environments (for example, in the North Sea), require
weather-vaning capabilities and have mooring lines attached to a turret.

               Recent finds of hot, sour, high pressure hydrocarbons have tilted the balance towards a slight preference for
               tapered stress joints. With various considerations influencing floating production system hull selection, a
               range of parameters can drive the eventual riser hang-off design and sometimes leads to a need for a longer
               stress joint that is better able to cope with high bending angle or higher fatigue loads. The high flexibility of
               titanium makes titanium TSJ’s an effective alternative to very long steel TSJ’s that can control the curvature
               of a riser’s hang-off region to the same extent. This increased market demand for titanium tapered stress joints
               has, at times, placed a considerable demand on a limited supply chain affecting cost. The cost of titanium is
               much greater than that of steel. This serves as a commercial stimulus either                                                                                           to reduce the cost of the titanium
               TSJ or to reduce the size of an equivalent steel TSJ.

               Reducing the cost of titanium TSJ’s could be achieved by only using titanium for curvature control and using
               another material for the (flanged) connection point. For many years shrink-fitting has been a standard
               connection method in which a shaft is inserted into a pre-heated female component which is then left to cool.
               Although common in many industries, the use of shrink-fitting in production riser component fabrication is
               relatively new. Welding remains the primary pipe connection method. This paper describes qualification
               testing conducted to understand the structural integrity of a shrink-fitted steel flange on titanium pipe and how
               the assembly behaves in high load, fatigue driven applications.

2                                                                                                                              INTRODUCTION

               The body of work that is currently being carried out to qualify a shrink fit steel-titanium joint builds on the
               work previously carried out by Subsea Riser Products Ltd to qualify a steel-steel shrink-fit, full bore (19in
               internal diameter), 10ksi drilling riser for use in the North Sea [1]. The design work and testing for this riser is
               complete and at the time of writing, the production phase is drawing to a close, with the first riser joints being
               delivered.

               It was noted early in the project that since the shrink-fit solution negates the need for welding, then it could be
               used to join high strength, thick walled, or dissimilar materials. Welding steel to titanium is not possible, so
               clearly this technique, properly developed and qualified, can provide a unique solution for joining titanium
               pipe to steel flanges.

               A well known example of titanium being used in an offshore drilling riser is the Heidrun Drilling Riser, which
               had riser pipe, flanges, booster line and fasteners all fabricated from titanium. The mean water depth that the
               riser was designed to drill at was 345m, and the material qualification and fabrication of this design lasted 4.5
               years. This is an expensive and time consuming way of producing an entire riser, and whilst risers fabricated
               entirely form titanium may find certain niches, it is much more common to find titanium in targeted areas of a
               riser system. In curvature controlled high stress areas, a low Young’s modulus in conjunction with high yield
               stress can be used to give technical advantage. An example of such an area would be production riser SCR
               hang-off locations. In these situations, the stresses imparted to the joints due to bending through a pre-defined
               angle are greatly reduced – improving the fatigue performance of the riser zone.

Abstract
Atlantis is a giant oil field with challenges that require a multi-disciplinary and phased approach to reservoir development.
Initial development focused on the better-imaged extra-salt segment of the structure after eight appraisal penetrations
revealed over a 1,500 ft oil column contained in several high quality thick pay sands.  Signals of the reservoir complexity that
would be associated with Atlantis were seen from the beginning.  The early wells found variable fluid contacts, fluid
compositional variations, large previously undetected faults, and what turned out to be perched water.  Development drilling
continued while the facilities were being fabricated.  The drilling results strengthened confidence that there were large in-
place resources but heightened concerns about complexity.  In response, the development plan was modified to include
ocean-bottom-seismic, downhole-flow-control completions, and a second production drill center.  Initial reservoir
performance revealed sub-seismic baffles that resulted in lower stabilized well productivity and more complex
compartmentalization than expected.  Integrated analyses of static and dynamic data enabled the integrated team to
demonstrate that recovery per well was similar to pre-drill expectation and modification to the development plan would allow
sustained production growth.  Challenges going forward include appraisal and development of remaining segments of the
field to effectively grow production and extend production plateau, and efficient operation of the wells, subsea architecture
and production facilities.

Introduction
This paper focuses on the subsurface challenges involved in appraising and developing Atlantis, a giant subsalt deepwater oil
field in the Gulf of Mexico.  Significant  uncertainty about the resource in less appraised sectors, the level of aquifer support,
and root cause of the observed static complexities indicated the development scheme required flexibility.

A phased approach focused initially on development of the extra salt area of the reservoir while providing the flexibility to
develop the subsalt sector and expand the topside capacity based on the actual reservoir outcome.

The results to date indicate this flexible phased approach was an efficient way to manage uncertainty while realizing value
from a large resource base.  Even after two years of production and continuous rig activity, there are sectors requiring furthe   r
appraisal and significant uncertainty still remains. This paper will touch on how the learnings from available data were used
to make development decisions while still retaining some flexibility to deal with remaining uncertainty.

Background
The Atlantis Field, discovered in 1998, is located approximately 190 miles south of New Orleans in the Gulf of Mexico
(Figure 1).  Atlantis is one of several deepwater hydrocarbon discoveries located in the southern Green Canyon protraction
area.  The Atlantis hydrocarbon accumulation is contained with in a large salt cored anticlinal fold.  Atlantis is situated
beneath the Sigsbee Escarpment, a major bathymetric feature associated with the overlying edge of allochthonous salt as it
approaches the seafloor.  Complex sea-floor topography plunges from 4,500 ft to 7,000 ft water depth at slopes up to 30 deg.
Two thirds of the Atlantis structure is located subsalt, and is therefore seismically obscured.  Several Miocene hydrocarbon
bearing reservoirs are present over the structure at depths of 16,000 to 19,000 ft subsea (Figure 2).  The main subsea drill
center for Atlantis is positioned at the base of the Sigsbee Escarpment.

Abstract
The BP-operated Thunder Horse and Atlantis developments are giants among the deepwater subsalt fields.  It was recognized
that effective development of these large fields would require a step-change improvement in the seismic imaging.   Through
close cooperation between asset and R&D teams, BP has pursued a two-pronged approach to deliver improved seismic
imaging for these and other subsalt deepwater fields.   New   seismic acquisition and new processing techniques were needed
to significantly improve the subsalt image.  The methods of acquisition and processing applied to each field are very different
and are dependent on field-specific issues that include: the timing and pace of development, existing seismic data,
infrastructure, seafloor bathymetry, salt geometry, and reservoir configuration.  Thunder Horse initiated an aggressive
anisotropic reprocessing project incorporating three independent 3-D seismic surveys in a multi-azimuth processing
sequence. Atlantis pursued a new 4-component ocean-bottom-node technology to provide uniform wide-azimuth acquisition,
and then pioneered new receiver-centric processing to image the data.  Both implementations yielded dramatic seismic image
improvement while highlighting additional challenges.

Abstract

While much focus is given to the challenges of designing and manufacturing riser systems for extreme deep waters, the
challenges are certainly not less when one tries to push the limit at the other end of the spectrum: in very shallow water. Due to
their advantages FPSO’s are being used in increasingly shallow waters (less than 50m water depth is current practice in
Vietnam now days). This puts real challenges on the mooring and riser designers together with FPSO contractors and forces
them to come up with novel configuration designs in particular when the very shallow water is combined with harsh
environmental conditions and significant vessel motions. An active collaboration between the mooring and the riser designers
is then of upmost importance, and requires validation of the concept at the earliest stage of the project: during FEED studies.

The main challenges reside in the need to accommodate the two extreme positions of the surface floater (Far/Ballasted and
Near/loaded) which often result in contradicting requirements. Interference is also a main concern, be it with the hull of the
FPSO, the seabed, the free water surface or other risers. Marine growth is also a critical issue as it impacts the riser
configuration on the full length. To adequately address all those requirements, novel, generally complex, configurations are
needed using combinations of clump weights, tethers, buoyancy elements and rigid or flexible structural members.

This paper will present and discuss the different issues faced when designing flexible riser systems in these very shallow
waters and present a number of novel solutions to address those. It will also present some actual field experience on two very
shallow water riser systems installed over the last two years and will explain how the designer reached the specific chosen
solution.

Introduction

This paper will concentrate on challenges of flexible riser systems design (this is mainly focusing on unbonded flexible pipes
but may be fully applied to umbilical) in very shallow waters, typically around 50m water depth.

Unbonded Flexible pipes are key elements for offshore oil & gas production, enabling connection of subsea wellhead to
floating platforms in shallow to ultra deep water fields.  Design of these risers is a complex and long iterative process; desi gn
criteria are well defined in relevant codes and standards (See Ref. [1], [2]).
